name: TTP-PERSONA

attribution.legal_posture: Official regional guidance covering a regional pattern; named actor, employer, account, and front company remain unreported.

ttps: Forged/stolen IDs, synthetic KYC documents, stolen or AI-generated faces, face swaps, false education/employment histories, identity rental, verified-account purchases, email/phone masking, and mutually fabricated reviews.
caveats: Nationality, accent, appearance, contractor status and remote work are context signals; attribution requires corroboration.
This is an official Japanese framing of already documented identity-fraud and laptop-farm methods; it supplies methods context rather than a new named network.

statements: PSIA gives the fraudulent-employment model a standalone hidden-threat treatment. It describes workers falsifying nationality, names and employment histories or impersonating real people to obtain freelance remote development work. It also describes U.S.-based helpers procuring false identity materials, operating laptop farms, receiving payroll and forwarding funds, while warning that contractors as well as employees can create sanctions and insider-access risk.

sources.support: OFSI describes false personae and aliases, rented identities, proxy accounts, fraudulent documents, face-swapping, and third parties completing verification or interviews
The UN Panel reports multiple fake personas, purchased or borrowed reputable accounts, synthetic supporting documents, proxy email/SMS services, and AI-generated profile images
sources.locator: Annex 64 (PDF pp. 354-359) | Original official publication page: https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n24/038/01/pdf/n2403801.pdf

sources.support: MSMT documents false and stolen identities, purchased or borrowed high-reputation accounts, proxy email/SMS services, and AI-generated profile material
sources.locator: report pp. 31-39; Annex 15 | Original official publication page: https://msmt.info/Publications/detail/MSMT%20Report/4221

sources.support: The Japanese alert lists identity-document misuse, proxy interview participation, and inconsistent or shared account details as warning signs
The joint alert describes forged or stolen identity material, AI-assisted identity obfuscation, and fabricated employment profiles

Japan's PSIA describes concealed DPRK IT workers using false nationality, names, work histories, or real-person impersonation to obtain remote freelance work, supported by U.S.-based helpers who procure identity materials, host employer laptops, enable remote access, receive payroll, and forward funds. It frames contractor access and payments as sanctions and insider-risk concerns, not as proof from remote status alone
sources.locator: Cyber section, PDF page 5, printed page 39, Column 2: 隠れた脅威：リモートワーカーに紛れ込む北朝鮮IT労働者

sources.support: BfV describes fictitious or stolen identities, forged identity and education documents, AI-generated or edited photographs, and false career histories
